definition: A hierarchical data structure of nodes joined by edges, with one root node and every other node having exactly one parent, so there are no cycles. File systems, the HTML DOM, organisation charts and parsed expressions are all trees.
example: A tree of 8 nodes always has exactly 7 edges, one per non-root node.

definition: The single node at the top of a tree, the only node with no parent. Every other node can be reached by following child links down from it, and its depth is 0.
example: In a file system the root directory / is the tree's root.

definition: A tree node with no children. Leaves have height 0; in a binary tree a leaf has two empty (None) child slots.
example: In a binary heap of n items, the last ⌈n/2⌉ array slots are all leaves.

definition: The node directly above a given node in a tree, connected to it by one edge. Every node except the root has exactly one parent.
example: In an array-stored binary heap, the parent of index 9 is at index 4.

definition: A node directly below another node in a tree, connected to it by one edge. In a binary tree each node has at most two children, called the left child and the right child.
example: In a BST, the left child of 50 holds a smaller key such as 30.

definition: Nodes that share the same parent in a tree. A heap or BST puts no ordering rule between siblings beyond what the structure's own invariant says.
example: If B, C and D are all children of A, they are siblings.

definition: A node of a tree together with all of its descendants, which is itself a tree with that node as its root. Most recursive tree algorithms solve a problem for each subtree and combine the answers.
example: In a BST every key in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node's key.

definition: Any node on the path from a given node up to the root: its parent, its parent's parent, and so on. Some definitions, including the one used for lowest common ancestors, count a node as its own ancestor.
example: In a file system, /home and / are ancestors of /home/alice/notes.txt.

definition: Any node reachable by going downwards from a given node: its children, their children, and so on. A node plus all its descendants forms its subtree.
example: Every node in a tree is a descendant of the root.

definition: The number of children a node has. In a binary tree every node has degree 0, 1 or 2; a leaf has degree 0.
example: A node with three children has degree 3.

definition: The number of edges on the path from the root down to a node. The root has depth 0 and its children depth 1; the greatest depth of any node equals the tree's height.
example: A key found after visiting 4 nodes in a BST sits at depth 3.

definition: For a node, the number of edges on the longest path from it down to a leaf; for a tree, the height of its root. With this edge-counting convention a leaf has height 0 and an empty tree height −1; some books count nodes instead and get one more.
example: A perfect binary tree of 15 nodes has height 3; a chain of 15 nodes has height 14.

definition: A binary tree in which every node has either 0 or 2 children, never exactly one. It always has one more leaf than internal node, so its node count is odd.
example: A full binary tree with 15 leaves has 14 internal nodes and 29 nodes in total.

definition: A binary tree in which every level is completely filled except possibly the last, and the last level is filled from left to right with no gaps. This shape is what lets a binary heap be stored in an array with no wasted slots.
example: A complete binary tree with a million nodes has height 19.

definition: A binary tree in which every internal node has two children and all leaves are at the same depth, so every level is full. A perfect tree of height h has exactly 2^(h+1) − 1 nodes.
example: Perfect trees have 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, … nodes.

definition: A binary tree in which, at every node, the heights of the left and right subtrees differ by at most 1. AVL trees maintain exactly this rule, which keeps the height logarithmic in the number of nodes.
example: A root whose left subtree has height 2 and right subtree height 0 is not height-balanced.

definition: A tree in which every internal node has only one child, so it is really a linked list: n nodes have height n − 1. Inserting sorted keys into a plain binary search tree produces one, and operations that should take O(log n) then take O(n).
example: Inserting 1, 2, 3, …, 1,000 into an empty plain BST gives a right-leaning chain of height 999.

definition: Storing a complete binary tree in a plain array in level order, with no pointers: the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2 and its parent at ⌊(i − 1)/2⌋ (0-based). It is compact and cache-friendly but wastes slots on sparse, unbalanced shapes.
example: Binary heaps such as Python's heapq use this layout.

definition: A way to store a tree whose nodes can have any number of children using only two pointers per node: one to its first child and one to its next sibling. It turns any rooted tree into a binary tree.
example: A directory with five subfolders points to the first; each subfolder points to the next.

definition: An extra field in a tree node that points back up to its parent. It makes walking upwards (for example to find a successor or the path to the root) easy, at the cost of one more pointer per node and extra bookkeeping on every change.
example: The Linux kernel's red-black trees keep a parent pointer in each node.

definition: The largest number of nodes on any single level of a tree. Breadth-first traversal's queue grows with the width, so it needs O(width) memory.
example: The last level of a perfect tree with 1,048,575 nodes holds 524,288 nodes.

definition: A set of vertices joined by edges that have no direction: an edge between A and B can be followed either way. It is connected when every vertex can reach every other; a connected undirected graph with no cycles is a tree.
example: A road map with two-way streets is an undirected graph.

definition: A path through a graph that starts and ends at the same vertex without reusing an edge. Trees have no cycles; a tree with a cycle would let a traversal loop for ever.
example: Pointing a child's link back at its grandparent creates a cycle.

definition: Containing no cycles. A tree is a connected acyclic graph; a directed acyclic graph (DAG) may still have nodes with several parents.

One of the points of a graph, joined to others by edges; in a tree, vertices are usually called nodes. Graph-algorithm costs are often written in terms of V, the number of vertices, and E, the number of edges.
example: Dijkstra's algorithm with a Fibonacci heap runs in O(E + V log V).

definition: A number attached to a graph edge, such as a distance or cost. Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm requires all edge weights to be nonnegative.
A graph whose edges have a direction and that contains no directed cycles. Unlike a tree, a node can have several parents, so two nodes can have more than one 'lowest' common ancestor.
example: Git's commit history is a DAG: a merge commit has two parents.

definition: A depth-first traversal that visits a node before its subtrees: node, left, right. It suits copying and serialising a tree, because a parent is always seen before its children.
example: Pre-order of a tree with root F, left B and right G starts F, B, ….

definition: A depth-first traversal of a binary tree that visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. On a binary search tree it yields the keys in sorted order.
example: In-order on a BST holding 20, 30, 40 visits 20, 30, 40.

definition: A depth-first traversal that visits both subtrees before the node itself: left, right, node. It suits any computation where a node's answer depends on its children's, such as heights, sizes, freeing memory and evaluating expression trees.
example: Post-order of the expression tree for (2 + 3) × 4 is 2 3 + 4 ×.

definition: A breadth-first traversal that visits nodes level by level, left to right: the root, then all depth-1 nodes, and so on. It uses a first-in, first-out queue.
example: Level-order is also the order in which a heap is stored in its array.

definition: An in-order traversal that needs only O(1) extra space, published by Joseph M. Morris in 1979. It temporarily points empty right pointers back to in-order successors ('threads') instead of using a stack, then removes them, so the tree is briefly modified.
A binary tree whose otherwise empty child pointers are reused as 'threads' pointing to a node's in-order predecessor or successor, so the tree can be walked in order without a stack.
example: Morris traversal creates threads temporarily and removes them as it goes.

definition: The node that comes immediately after a given node in in-order (sorted) order. In a BST it is the leftmost node of the right subtree if there is one; otherwise the nearest ancestor whose left subtree contains the node.
example: In a BST holding 30, 35, 40, the in-order successor of 30 is 35.

definition: The node that comes immediately before a given node in in-order (sorted) order; in a BST it is the rightmost node of the left subtree when that exists. It can replace a deleted two-child node just as well as the successor.

An object that yields a binary search tree's keys in sorted order one at a time, using an explicit stack of pending ancestors instead of recursion. Each advance costs O(1) amortised, and memory is proportional to the tree's height.

A tree whose leaves are numbers or variables and whose internal nodes are operators applied to their children. Evaluating it is a post-order traversal; printing it in post-order gives Reverse Polish Notation.
example: (2 + 3) × 4 becomes a × node with children + (over 2 and 3) and 4.

definition: The number of edges on the shortest path from the root to any leaf. Breadth-first search finds it efficiently because it can stop at the first leaf it dequeues.
The list of nodes you would see looking at a binary tree from the right: the last node on each level. It is found with a level-order traversal that records the last node of each round.
The C standard-library function that returns a block of heap memory to the allocator. After free, the block must not be read or written again.
example: Freeing a tree node before reading its child pointers is a use-after-free bug.

definition: A bug in which a program reads or writes memory after it has been freed. The memory may already hold other data, so the result is unpredictable and often a security hole.
example: Freeing a node and then reading node->right is a use-after-free.

definition: A low-level compiled programming language from the early 1970s in which memory is managed by hand with malloc and free. Operating-system kernels such as Linux are written in it.
The Unix command that reports how much disk space a directory uses, adding up its files and subdirectories: a post-order computation over the directory tree.
example: du -sh ~/Downloads prints the total size of that folder.

definition: The Unix command that deletes a directory and everything inside it recursively. It must delete a directory's contents before the directory itself, which is post-order.
A Python function containing yield that produces values one at a time on demand instead of building a whole list. A recursive generator still uses one stack frame per level of recursion.

The rule that makes a binary tree a binary search tree: for every node, all keys in its left subtree are smaller and all keys in its right subtree are larger. It applies to whole subtrees, not just to a node's immediate children.
example: A 6 sitting anywhere in the right subtree of 10 breaks the BST property even if its parent is 15.

definition: An ordering in which any two different values can be compared and one is definitely smaller, consistently and transitively. Search trees and heaps assume their keys have one.
example: Floating-point NaN breaks total order: it is neither smaller, larger nor equal to anything.

definition: A special floating-point value representing an undefined result such as 0/0. Every <, > or == comparison involving NaN is false (only != is true), so NaN keys break sorting and search-tree invariants.
example: float('nan') < 5 and float('nan') > 5 are both False in Python.

definition: Special floating-point values larger (or, for minus infinity, smaller) than every ordinary number. They make convenient starting bounds, for example the initial range when validating a BST.
example: In Python, float('-inf') < -10**300 is True.

definition: The middle value of a sorted list: half the values are below it and half above. Choosing the median key as the root at each level builds a perfectly balanced BST from sorted data.
example: The median of 1, 3, 7, 8, 9 is 7.

definition: The standard way to delete a node with two children from a BST: replace it with its in-order successor and delete that successor instead. Always using the successor slowly skews a tree under long random insert/delete sequences.

Changing a few child or parent pointers so that a node or subtree takes a new position in the tree, without copying keys. Production BSTs relink nodes on deletion so that references to other nodes stay valid.
example: Deleting a one-child node splices its child into its place by relinking one pointer.

definition: A search tree that automatically restructures itself after inserts and deletes (usually with rotations) so its height stays O(log n) whatever order keys arrive in. AVL and red-black trees are the classic examples.
A BST built by inserting distinct keys in a uniformly random order. A uniformly chosen key then has expected depth about 2 ln n ≈ 1.39 log₂ n, and the expected height is also logarithmic.
example: For a million random keys the average depth is about 25.

definition: The mathematical constant e ≈ 2.71828, the base of the natural logarithm.

The inverse of raising to a power: the base-b logarithm of x is the power you raise b to in order to get x. In algorithms the base is usually 2, so it counts how many times n can be halved; log₂ of a million is about 20.
The function that rounds a number down to the nearest whole number, written ⌊x⌋. Python's // operator performs floor division.
The function that rounds a number up to the nearest whole number, written ⌈x⌉.
example: ⌈4.5⌉ = 5, so a heap of 9 items has ⌈9/2⌉ = 5 leaves.

definition: The size of a number ignoring its sign, written |x|. |−2| = 2 and |2| = 2.
example: An AVL node is balanced when |height(left) − height(right)| ≤ 1.

definition: Θ(f(n)) means a cost grows exactly as fast as f(n), up to constant factors: it is bounded both above and below by multiples of f(n). It is stricter than Big O, which only gives an upper bound.
example: Building a plain BST from sorted keys costs Θ(n²) node visits.

definition: Big O notation for work that grows in proportion to a tree's height h, such as following one root-to-leaf path. It is O(log n) on a balanced tree of n nodes but O(n) on a degenerate chain.
example: Searching a BST of height 3 visits at most 4 nodes.

definition: Big O notation for work that grows in proportion to L, the length of a key in characters. Trie lookups are O(L), independent of how many keys are stored.
example: Looking up a 7-letter word in a trie takes at most 7 steps.

definition: A value recording when something happened, such as seconds since 1970. Timestamps usually arrive in increasing order, which is exactly the input that turns a plain BST into a chain.
A pure-Python library providing sorted list, dict and set types. Instead of a balanced tree it keeps a list of sorted sublists.
A sorted linked list with extra randomly chosen 'express lane' levels of links, giving expected O(log n) search, insert and delete. Redis sorted sets can use one.

A constant-time local restructuring of a binary search tree that moves one node up and its parent down while preserving the in-order (sorted) order. Self-balancing trees use rotations to fix imbalance after updates.
example: A right rotation at y lifts its left child x; x's right subtree becomes y's left subtree.

definition: The first self-balancing binary search tree (Adelson-Velsky and Landis, 1962). At every node the left and right subtree heights differ by at most 1, which keeps the height below about 1.44 log₂ n.
example: A million-key AVL tree is at most 27 edges tall.

definition: In an AVL tree, a node's left subtree height minus its right subtree height. AVL trees require it to be −1, 0 or +1 at every node and rotate when an update makes it ±2.
example: A node with an empty left side and a right subtree of height 1 has balance factor −2.

term: AVL rebalancing cases (LL, RR, LR, RL)
definition: The four shapes an AVL insert can create, named after the path from the unbalanced node to the new key: LL and RR need one rotation, while the zig-zag LR and RL cases need a double rotation.
example: Inserting 30, 10, 20 creates the LR case: rotate left at 10, then right at 30.

definition: In a red-black tree, the empty child positions, treated as black leaf nodes that hold no key. Counting them makes the black-height rule uniform.
In a red-black tree, the number of black nodes on any path from a node down to a NIL leaf; the rules make it the same on every such path. Books differ on whether the starting node itself is counted.
The sibling of a node's parent. Red-black insertion decides between recolouring and rotating by looking at the colour of the new node's uncle.
The parent of a node's parent. Red-black and AVL fix-ups often rotate around the grandparent.
Changing the red/black colours of nodes during a red-black tree fix-up without moving any nodes. It costs O(1) per step but can repeat up the tree, O(log n) times in one update.

A balanced search tree in which each node holds 1, 2 or 3 keys and has 2, 3 or 4 children, with all leaves at the same depth. Every red-black tree corresponds to one: glue each black node to its red children.
A balanced search tree whose nodes hold 1 or 2 keys and have 2 or 3 children, with all leaves at the same depth. Left-leaning red-black trees can be set up to correspond to 2-3 trees.
A simpler variant of the red-black tree introduced by Robert Sedgewick in 2008 that only allows red links to lean left, which cuts the number of fix-up cases and shortens the code.
An American computer scientist at Princeton, co-author of the textbook Algorithms (with Kevin Wayne) and co-inventor of the red-black tree formulation (with Leonidas Guibas, 1978).

A container whose link fields (child, parent, colour) are embedded inside the objects it stores rather than in separately allocated nodes. Given an object you already have its node, so it can be removed without a search.
example: Each Linux task embeds its own red-black tree node.

definition: The Linux kernel's generic intrusive red-black tree implementation, used by the scheduler, memory management, epoll and many other subsystems.
The Linux process scheduler from version 2.6.23. It kept runnable tasks in a red-black tree ordered by virtual runtime and ran the leftmost task; Linux began replacing it with EEVDF in 6.6.
Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First, the fair-scheduling algorithm Linux began adopting in version 6.6 in place of CFS. Its implementation uses an augmented red-black tree.
In Linux fair scheduling, a task's CPU time scaled by its priority weight. CFS always ran the task with the smallest vruntime, the one that had received least.
The component that decides which job, task or process runs next. Priority queues (heaps) or ordered trees typically hold the waiting work.
The C++ standard library's ordered associative containers. The standard requires O(log n) operations and stable iterators; libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC all implement them as red-black trees.
The C++ standard library implementation from the LLVM project, used by Clang on macOS and elsewhere.
Microsoft's C and C++ compiler and standard library for Windows.
Java's sorted set class, backed by a TreeMap and so by a red-black tree, giving O(log n) add, remove and contains.
Java NavigableMap methods that find the nearest key at or below (floorKey), at or above (ceilingKey) or strictly above (higherKey) a given key, in O(log n) on a TreeMap.
The official API documentation generated from comments in Java source code; for the standard library it states guarantees such as TreeMap's O(log n) operations.
The collection of data structures and functions that ships with a programming language, such as Python's heapq or C++'s std::map.
A binary search tree in which each node also gets a random priority, kept in heap order. The randomness makes the expected height O(log n) whatever order keys arrive in.
A workload in which most operations modify data (write-heavy) or most only read it (read-heavy). It guides choices such as red-black versus AVL trees, which trade rotation cost for lookup depth.
Restoring heap order after adding an item at the bottom: swap it with its parent while it is smaller (in a min-heap). It makes at most one swap per level, O(log n).
example: Pushing 0 into a heap of 8 items sifts it up 3 levels to the root.

definition: Restoring heap order from the top: swap an item with its smaller child (in a min-heap) until it is no larger than both children. Used by pop and by bottom-up heapify; at most one swap per level.

Building a heap from n unsorted items by sifting down every non-leaf, from the last one back to the root. It takes O(n), faster than n separate pushes, because most nodes sit near the bottom and move only a short way.
The C++ standard library's general sorting function. Major implementations use introsort, guaranteeing O(n log n) comparisons.
A priority-queue operation that lowers an existing item's priority and repositions it. Python's heapq lacks it, so code pushes a new entry and lazily ignores the old one instead.

Marking an entry as removed instead of removing it immediately, and skipping it when it is later encountered. With heaps it replaces decrease-key: push the updated entry and discard stale ones as they pop.
heapq functions that combine a pop and a push in one O(log n) operation: heapreplace pops the smallest then pushes, heappushpop pushes then pops. Both are faster than separate calls.
heapq helpers that return the k largest or smallest items of an iterable, using a size-k heap internally where that is efficient.
example: heapq.nlargest(3, [5, 1, 9, 3, 7]) returns [9, 7, 5].

definition: A lazy k-way merge in Python's heapq: given several sorted inputs, it yields one sorted stream using a small heap of their current heads.
Python 3.14's max-heap counterpart to heapq.heapify, alongside heappush_max, heappop_max and related functions.
Sorting data too large for memory: sort memory-sized chunks into sorted runs on disk, then k-way merge the runs.
example: 1,024 sorted runs holding 10⁹ records are merged with a heap of 1,024 run heads.

definition: A heap in which each node has d children instead of 2. It is shallower, so push is cheaper and cache use better, but each sift-down level compares d children.
A priority queue with amortised O(1) insert and decrease-key and O(log n) delete-min, which gives Dijkstra's algorithm O(E + V log V) time. Its constant factors are large in practice.
A simple self-adjusting heap made of a multiway tree, often fast in practice; its decrease-key amortised cost is analysed differently from a Fibonacci heap's.
A priority queue of pending timers ordered by expiry time, so the earliest timer to fire is always at the front.
Go's standard-library heap package: it provides heap operations over any type implementing Len, Less, Swap, Push and Pop.
The fixed multiplier that Big O notation ignores: an algorithm doing 3n steps and one doing 30n are both O(n), but the second is ten times slower.
A boolean stored in a trie node marking that a stored key ends there. It is needed because a key can be a prefix of another key, so 'is a leaf' is not enough.
example: In a trie holding do and dog, the o node has its end-of-word flag set.

definition: The number of distinct symbols keys can contain, written σ: 26 for lowercase English letters, 256 for bytes. An array-of-children trie reserves σ pointers per node.
A query for all stored keys that start with a given string. Tries answer it by walking to the prefix's node and listing everything below it; hash tables must scan every key.
example: Autocomplete for "inte" is a prefix query.

definition: A compressed binary trie (Practical Algorithm To Retrieve Information Coded In Alphanumeric, Morrison 1968) in which single-child chains are collapsed, so each internal node branches. It is the binary form of a radix tree.
Choosing where to send each Internet Protocol packet by looking up its destination address in a routing table of address prefixes, picking the longest matching prefix.
Choosing, among all stored prefixes that match a key, the longest (most specific) one. Routers use it to pick a route; a trie finds it by walking down and remembering the last stored prefix passed.
Classless Inter-Domain Routing: writing an IP address block as address/length, where the length says how many leading bits are fixed. 10.1.0.0/16 covers every address starting 10.1.
The protocol that addresses and routes packets across the Internet. An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four numbers (octets) such as 10.1.3.7.
A group of 8 bits; each of the four dot-separated numbers (0–255) in an IPv4 address is one octet.
example: In 10.1.3.7 the third octet is 3, binary 00000011.

definition: The route a router uses when no more specific prefix matches, written 0.0.0.0/0 in IPv4.
A level-compressed trie: a binary trie where dense regions are replaced by multi-way nodes, cutting depth. Linux's IPv4 routing table (fib_trie) uses one.
A fast HTTP request router for Go that matches URL paths using a radix tree.
The part of a web framework that maps a request's URL path (such as /api/v1/users) to the code that handles it, often with a radix tree.
Redis's compact serialised encoding for a small list of strings or numbers in one memory block. Redis Streams store groups of entries as listpacks inside a radix tree.
A public blockchain platform. It stores account state in a Merkle Patricia trie so any part of the state can be verified by hash.
A radix trie in which each node is identified by a cryptographic hash of its contents, so a single root hash fingerprints the whole data set. Ethereum uses it for its world state.
The Linux kernel's array-like data structure, internally a radix tree, which superseded the kernel's older radix-tree API. The page cache uses it to map file offsets to memory pages.

A trie variant in which each node holds one character and three children: less than, equal to, and greater than that character. It uses far less memory than array-of-children tries and still supports prefix search.
A compressed trie of every suffix of a text. It answers 'does pattern P occur in the text?' in time proportional to P's length, and can be built in linear time.
A sorted array of the starting positions of all suffixes of a text: a more space-efficient alternative to a suffix tree for substring search.
The end part of a string: "ation" is a suffix of "application". The whole string and the empty string are also suffixes.

An algorithm (Aho and Corasick, 1975) that finds every occurrence of many patterns in one pass over a text, using a trie of the patterns plus failure links that say where to continue after a mismatch.
The Unix command that searches text for fixed strings rather than regular expressions; the original was built on the Aho–Corasick algorithm.
The operating system developed at Bell Labs from 1969, whose tools and design (files, pipes, small commands) shaped Linux and macOS.
Security software that inspects network traffic or system activity for signs of attack, often by matching thousands of known attack signatures at once.
A finite-state machine that produces output as it reads input. Search libraries use them as compact dictionaries that share both prefixes and suffixes of keys.
Language-aware rules for sorting text, which can differ from simple code-point order (for example placing é next to e).
One digit of a base-16 (hexadecimal) number: 0–9 then a–f, each standing for 4 bits.
example: A SHA-256 value written in hex is 64 hex digits.

definition: A cryptographic hash function that maps any input to a 256-bit value, usually written as 64 hex digits. Its outputs look uniformly random, so a million of them share almost no long prefixes.
The deepest node that has both of two given nodes as descendants (a node counts as its own descendant). It underlies distance queries and 'how are these related?' questions in hierarchies.
example: In a BST with root 6, the LCA of 0 and 5 is 2.

definition: The most widely used version-control system. It stores history as a DAG of commits.
A snapshot of a project in Git, linked to its parent commit(s); a merge commit has two parents.
The best common ancestor commit of two Git branches, used as the starting point for a three-way merge. Because history is a DAG, there can be several.
Precomputing each node's ancestors 1, 2, 4, 8, … levels up (O(n log n) time and space) so that any climb, and hence any LCA query, takes O(log n) jumps.
example: A 100,000-node tree needs 17 levels of jumps.

definition: A sequence that records each node when a depth-first walk enters it and again after returning from each child. The LCA of two nodes is the shallowest node between their first appearances, which turns LCA into a range-minimum query.
Finding the smallest value in a contiguous slice of an array. With a sparse table, each query takes O(1) after O(n log n) preprocessing.
A precomputed table storing the minimum (or another overlap-safe answer) of every array range whose length is a power of two, enabling O(1) range-minimum queries after O(n log n) work.
A binary tree over an array in which each node stores a summary (sum, minimum, …) of a range, supporting range queries and updates in O(log n).
A compact array-based structure that maintains prefix sums with O(log n) updates and queries.
The number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes of a tree. That path need not pass through the root; it bends at its highest node.
The total of the values on a path through a tree. Common problems ask whether a root-to-leaf path reaches a target, how many downward paths do, or what the largest path sum is.
The largest total of values along any path in a tree, where values may be negative. It is computed in post-order, passing up the best one-sided gain and recording the best two-sided bend.
In the maximum-path-sum problem, the best sum of a path that starts at a node and goes down one side only. Negative gains are clamped to 0 because extending into them would only lower the total.
Forcing a value into a range by replacing anything outside it with the nearest limit, for example max(gain, 0) turns negative gains into 0.
A placeholder token, such as #, written for every empty child when serialising a tree, so the exact shape can be rebuilt. A binary tree of n nodes writes n + 1 of them.
example: The tree 1 → left 2 serialises as 1,2,#,#,#.

definition: A website of programming interview problems; its convention for displaying trees is level order with null for missing children.
The Python exception raised by next() when an iterator has no more items. In the lesson's deserialiser it signals truncated input.
A diagram of who reports to whom in an organisation. With one boss per person it is a tree rooted at the chief executive.
The most senior manager of a company; the root of its organisation chart.
The tree of objects a browser builds from a web page's HTML: each element is a node whose children are the elements nested inside it. Scripts read and change the page through it.
HyperText Markup Language, the markup that structures web pages. Its nested elements form a tree, the DOM.
A file-system container that holds files and other directories, forming a tree from the root directory down.
An extra directory entry pointing at the same file data, so one file can appear in several places; this means a file system is not strictly a tree.
A small file that points to another path. Following symbolic links can create cycles, so tree-walking tools must take care.
A controlled, repeatable measurement of how fast a piece of code runs on a stated workload and machine. Asymptotic bounds say how cost grows; benchmarks say which implementation is actually faster.
A link between two nodes of a tree or graph; in a rooted tree each edge joins a parent to one of its children. A tree of n nodes always has n − 1 edges, and depths and heights are counted in edges.
example: A tree of 8 nodes has 7 edges, one above every node except the root.

definition: A collection of separate trees: a graph with no cycles that need not be connected. A forest of n nodes made of c trees has n − c edges.
example: Two separate trees of 4 and 5 nodes form a forest with 9 nodes and 7 edges.

definition: A trie in which every chain of single-child nodes that does not mark a key end is merged into one edge labelled with a string. That bounds the node count at about 2n for n keys, whatever the key lengths.
example: car, card, care and cat fit in a radix tree of 5 labelled nodes plus the root.

definition: Turning a tree into a flat sequence of tokens (such as a comma-separated string) that can be stored or sent, and rebuilding the identical tree from it later. Writing a marker for every empty child in pre-order is one simple, unambiguous format.
example: The tree 3 → (9, 20 → (15, 7)) serialises in pre-order as 3,9,#,#,20,15,#,#,7,#,#.
